en: The *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Of the winter month, one night has passed and one night remains."
The moon is waning;
old age and death have drawn near, and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.
O Venerable Ones!
For the sake of attaining the Way, one should practice with single-minded diligence and vigor. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas, through single-minded diligence and vigor, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; how much more so for other wholesome dharmas of the Path!
“The one who has not yet received full ordination has already departed.
‘The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what should be done first?
One person should say:”
"Let us perform the Uposatha and recite the Prātimokṣa. Venerable sirs!
Let those bhikṣus who have not arrived announce their *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*."
“With palms joined, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas;
I now wish to recite the precepts—may the Saṃgha listen with a single mind!”
Even regarding minor offenses, one’s mind should feel great dread;
having committed a fault, one should repent with single-mindedness and never commit it again.
The horse of the mind gallops down evil paths; when abandoned to negligence, it is difficult to restrain.
The Buddha taught all the precepts and practices, Just like sharp reins and bits.
When the Buddha’s mouth speaks the instructions, The virtuous are able to believe and accept them;
Such a person has a well-trained steed, And can destroy the army of afflictions.
If one does not accept instruction, nor takes delight in the precepts,
this person’s horse is untamed and they are submerged in the army of afflictions.
If a person guards the precepts as a yak loves its tail;
Binding the mind with heedfulness, like a monkey bound by chains,
one should always exert oneself day and night for the sake of seeking true wisdom;
such a person within the Buddha-dharma is able to attain a pure livelihood.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today is the fifteenth day for the poṣadha and the recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its attention, let the Saṃgha with one mind perform the poṣadha and recite the Prātimokṣa. This is the formal motion."
"Venerable sirs!

We shall now perform the Poṣadha ceremony and recite the Prātimokṣa. May the Saṃgha listen with one mind: those who have committed an offense should confess it; those who are without offense should remain silent."
Because of their silence, it should be known that all the venerable ones are pure.
Just as this was the response for each individual monk, so too is it for the three proclamations made within this assembly of monks.
If there is a bhikṣu who, during such a third proclamation among this assembly of bhikṣus, remembers having committed an offense but does not disclose it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.
Venerable sirs!
Therefore, the Buddha has declared that the offense of lying is an obstructive dharma.

If a bhikṣu seeks purity within this regard, he should acknowledge his transgression if he remembers it; by acknowledging it, he will find peace, but by failing to acknowledge it, his offense becomes even deeper.
"Venerable sirs! The introduction to the Prātimokṣa has been recited. Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard?
He asks a second and a third time in the same manner.
"Is there purity herein? "Venerable sirs!
There is purity herein, because of your silence; thus it shall be held."
“Venerable sirs!
These four *pārājika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*.

If a bhikṣu, having entered into the dharma of the precepts with other bhikṣus, does not return his precepts and does not withdraw from them while they are weakened, yet commits the act of sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense and is no longer fit to participate in communal affairs.”
"If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in an open space, takes what is not given—this is called stealing property.
Because he has taken what was not given, the king or one equal to a king may seize him, kill him, bind him, banish him, or impose a fine;
or they may say to him: 'Hey!'"
"You childish one!
You fool! You thief!"
If a bhikṣu, having such characteristics, takes an object that was not given to him, this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and should not participate in communal affairs.

"If a bhikṣu, whether it be a human or one resembling a human, intentionally deprives them of life with his own hand, or provides a knife himself, or instructs another to provide one, or instructs them to die, or praises death, or speaks thus: 'Hey!'"
"What use is living a life of evil?
Death is better than life.

If, following that person's inclination toward death, one uses various causes and conditions to instruct them toward death or praise death, and that person dies as a result of this matter, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and should not participate in communal affairs.
"If a bhikṣu, being empty and possessing nothing, neither knowing nor seeing the superhuman states, the noble benefits, and the fulfillment, yet claims with knowledge or vision:
'I know thus; I see thus.'"
Later, whether that bhikṣu is questioned or not, for the sake of purifying himself by emerging from his offense, he says:
"I said I knew what I did not know; I said I saw what I did not see."
"Empty, deceptive, and false speech—this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bhikṣu, such that he should not participate in communal affairs;
except in the case of overweening pride. Venerable sirs!"

The four *pārājika* rules have now been explained. If a bhikṣu commits any one of these rules, that bhikṣu is not permitted to live in community nor to engage in communal affairs; as it was before, so it is after. This bhikṣu has incurred a *pārājika* offense and should not be engaged in communal affairs.
"Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter?
He asks a second and a third time in the same way:
"Are you pure in this matter?"
"Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held.
Venerable sirs!"
These thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, this bhikṣu commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense,
except in a dream."

"If a bhikṣu, with a mind corrupted by lust, engages in physical contact with a woman—whether grasping her hand, grasping her arm, grasping her hair, or grasping any individual part of her body, or stroking her from above or below, or touching her smooth skin—it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."

"If a bhikṣu, with a mind corrupted by lust, utters coarse, evil, and unwholesome words of sexual desire toward a woman, addressing her as a young man or woman would one another, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣu, with a mind corrupted by lust, in the presence of a woman, should praise his own person for the sake of offerings, saying:
'Sister! Like us bhikṣus, we uphold the precepts, have abandoned sexual desire, and practice the wholesome Dharma.'"
"Sisters!
The offering of the dharma of sexual desire is the foremost offering.
This constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

"If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between, conveying a man's intention to a woman or a woman's intention to a man, whether for the purpose of marriage or for illicit intercourse, even for a single act of sexual union, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣu, for his own sake and without a patron, seeks materials to build a hut, he should build it according to the prescribed measurement. This measurement for the hut is:

twelve *vitasti* of the Buddha’s spans in length and seven *vitasti* in internal width. That bhikṣu should take other bhikṣus with him and show them the site for building the hut, ensuring it is a place free from difficulties and not a place that causes obstruction."
The bhikṣus should point out a site for building a hut that is free from difficulties and not obstructive.

If a bhikṣu, for his own sake, solicits materials to build a hut on a site with difficulties or obstructions where there is no owner, and does not show the site to the bhikṣus, and it exceeds the prescribed measure, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

"If a bhikṣu, having a patron, wishes to build a large dwelling for himself, that bhikṣu should lead other bhikṣus to inspect the site for the dwelling to ensure it is a place free from difficulties and not a place of obstruction.
The bhikṣus should point out a site for building a hut that is free from difficulties and not obstructive.
If one builds a large hut for oneself on a site with difficulties or obstructions, or if it has an owner, and does not show the site to the bhikṣus, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and resentment, being displeased with a pure and faultless bhikṣu, should defame him with a groundless *pārājika* offense, desiring to destroy that bhikṣu’s pure conduct."
At a later time, whether that bhikṣu has been investigated or not, he knows that the matter was groundless.
Because it was groundless, that bhikṣu, abiding in a state of hatred, says to the other bhikṣus:
"I spoke thus because of my anger."
Saṃghāvaśeṣa.

"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, takes up a fragment or something resembling a fragment from a matter that is entirely different, and accuses a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a pārājika offense of a pārājika offense, desiring to destroy that bhikṣu’s pure conduct."

At a later time, whether that bhikṣu has been examined or not, he knows that this is a matter of a different category, a fragment taken from a matter of a different category, or a semblance of such a fragment.
If that bhikṣu, dwelling in a state of anger, says to the other bhikṣus,
"I spoke thus because of my anger," it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If a bhikṣu, for the sake of causing a schism in a harmonious Saṅgha, exerts himself with skillful means, or accepts the causes and conditions for such a schism and engages in dispute,
the other bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir!'"
Do not exert yourself in skillful means for the sake of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha, nor do you engage in disputes by accepting the causes that lead to such division.
Venerable One!
You should act in concert with the Saṃgha.
Why is this? Because the Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute; with one mind and one training, they dwell in peace and happiness like water and milk mixed together.
Venerable Sir!
"Abandon this matter which is a cause for schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus have thus admonished him, if he persists in that matter and does not abandon it, the bhikṣus should admonish him a second and a third time.
"It is well if he relinquishes this matter; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

This is the case where, for the sake of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha, a monk makes diligent efforts and employs stratagems. Other monks who are his close friends, of like mind, and acting in concert—whether one, two, or many of them—speak to the other monks, saying:
'Venerable sirs!'"
In this matter, do not admonish this bhikṣu.

Why? Because this bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma and speaks what is wholesome; this bhikṣu teaches the Dharma and does not teach what is contrary to the Dharma, he teaches what is wholesome and does not teach what is unwholesome; this bhikṣu speaks with knowledge and does not speak without knowledge.
"Whatever this bhikṣu says is exactly what we desire in our hearts; whatever this bhikṣu wishes to accept, we also wish to accept.
The bhikṣus should thus admonish those bhikṣus who agree with him:
"Venerable sirs, do not speak these words:"

"This bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma; this bhikṣu speaks well. This bhikṣu teaches the Dharma and does not teach what is contrary to the Dharma; he teaches what is wholesome and does not teach what is unwholesome. This bhikṣu speaks with knowledge and does not speak without knowledge. Whatever this bhikṣu says is exactly what our hearts desire; whatever this bhikṣu seeks to approve, we also seek to approve."
"Venerable Sir!
Do not take pleasure in assisting in the schism of the Saṃgha; you should instead take pleasure in assisting in the reconciliation of the Saṃgha. Why is this?"
The Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute; with one mind and one training, they dwell in peace and happiness like water and milk mixed together.
Venerable sirs, you should abandon any agreement to cause schism in the Saṃgha or any speech that promotes division.
When the monks thus admonish that monk who agrees with them, if he persists in that matter and does not relinquish it, the monks should admonish him a second and a third time.
"It is well if you abandon this matter; if you do not abandon it, there is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu resides in dependence upon a city or a village, and those bhikṣus therein commit evil deeds and defile the families of others, such that these acts are all seen, heard, and known."
The monks should thus admonish those monks:
"Venerable sirs!
Your evil conduct and your defiling of families have all been seen, heard, and known."
"Venerable sirs!
You should depart; you should not remain here.
Then that bhikṣu spoke to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
These bhikṣus act according to desire, hatred, fear, and delusion. Why is this?
"There may be monks who have committed such an identical offense, yet some are expelled while others are not.
The monks should say to that monk:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not speak these words:
"The bhikṣus follow favoritism, hatred, fear, and delusion; among bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not."
Why is this? Because the bhikṣus do not follow after craving, hatred, fear, or delusion.
O Venerable Ones!
"You all have committed evil deeds and defiled families; this is known by all through seeing, hearing, and awareness.
O Venerable Ones, abandon these words born of attachment, hatred, fear, and delusion.
You must depart; you should not remain here."
When the monks thus admonish that monk who agrees with them, if he persists in his position and does not relinquish it, the monks should admonish him a second and a third time.
"It is well if he relinquishes this matter; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

There was a bhikṣu of evil character who was difficult to speak with; the other bhikṣus should, in accordance with the Dharma and in a wholesome manner, speak to him regarding the matters of the *pratimokṣa* that he has transgressed."
One makes oneself unfit for conversation, speaking thus:
"Venerable sirs!
Do not speak to me of whether I am good or bad; I likewise shall not speak to you venerable sirs of whether you are good or bad. Venerable sirs, there is no need to admonish me."
The monks should admonish that monk:
"Venerable one!

The monks have spoken according to the Dharma and in accordance with what is wholesome regarding the matters of the *prātimokṣa* offenses you have committed; do not make yourself one who is beyond communal address, but rather make yourself one who is fit for communal address."

"Venerable sir, you should speak to the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with what is wholesome; the bhikṣus, in turn, should speak to you, venerable sir, in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with what is wholesome. Why is that?"
The assembly of all Tathāgatas increases in this way, namely, by speaking together, admonishing together, and emerging together from faults.
Venerable sir,
abandon this personal karma of refusing to speak with others.
When the bhikṣus have admonished him in this manner, if he persists in this matter and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should admonish him a second and a third time.
It is well if he relinquishes this matter; if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"Venerable sirs!

The thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas have been recited: nine offenses that are complete upon commission and four offenses for which there are up to three admonitions. If a bhikṣu commits any one of these offenses and knowingly conceals it, he shall, for however long the concealment lasted, be compelled to undergo *parivāsa*."
Having completed the *parivāsa*, that bhikṣu should undergo the *mānatva* for six days and six nights within the Saṃgha.
Having completed the *mānatva*, he next proceeds to the *ābhāṣaṇa*.
Once this has been performed according to the Dharma, the bhikṣus will be joyful. Within an assembly of twenty bhikṣus, the offense should be cleared.

If there is one person short and the assembly does not reach twenty, and they wish to clear this bhikṣu’s offense, that bhikṣu’s offense cannot be cleared; furthermore, the other bhikṣus may also be censured. Such is the nature of this rule.
"Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter?
He asks a second and a third time in the same manner.
"Venerable Ones!"
"In this matter, we are pure; because we are silent, let it be so held.
"Venerable sirs!
These two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharmas) are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa."
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place suitable for sexual intercourse,
a trustworthy upāsikā may charge that bhikṣu with one of three offenses:
either a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika."
If a bhikṣu says of himself,
"I sat in this place," he should be dealt with according to the Dharma as prescribed within the three methods:
Whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*, one shall treat that bhikṣu according to various other rules in accordance with what a trustworthy upāsikā has stated.
This is the first *aniyata-dharma*.

"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in a place that is not secluded or concealed, nor one where sexual intercourse is impossible, and this bhikṣu speaks coarse and lewd words of sexual desire to that woman."
A trustworthy female lay follower (upāsikā) may state one of two matters:
either a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense or a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu himself says:
"I sat in this place.
Regarding these two types of offenses, one should govern the bhikṣu according to the rule prescribed for each:
whether it be a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*, one should deal with that bhikṣu according to various other rules based on what the trustworthy upāsikā has said.
"These are the two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharma). Venerable sirs!
The two indeterminate rules have been recited; now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in regard to these?"
"A second and third time, he asks in the same manner:
'Venerable sirs!
Since you are pure in this matter, as indicated by your silence, let it be so held.'"
"Venerable sirs!
These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*.
'If a bhikṣu has completed his set of three robes during the period of the *kaṭhina* robe, he may keep an extra robe for up to ten days.'"
If one keeps them beyond that limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu,
having completed his set of three robes during the period of the *kaṭhina* robe, should stay overnight apart from any one of those three robes at another location, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*,
except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha."

"If a bhikṣu has completed his set of three robes during the period when the kaṭhina cloth is extended, and he obtains an out-of-season robe, that bhikṣu, if he requires a robe, may take the material with his own hands; he should quickly make it into a bhikṣu’s robe and keep it."

If he obtains enough, it is well; if he does not obtain enough, but knows of another place where it can be obtained, or for the sake of making it complete, that bhikṣu may keep this robe for up to one month.
If one keeps [an extra robe] for more than one month, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
except in exchange."
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash an old robe, or to dye it, or to beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu begs for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative and receives one, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*,
except in cases of [allowable] circumstances."
Regarding the "circumstances": being deprived of one's robes, having one's robes lost, having one's robes burned, or having one's robes carried away by water—these are called the circumstances.

"If a bhikṣu, having been deprived of his robes, having lost his robes, having had his robes burned, or having had his robes carried away by water, should beg for robes from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative."

If a householder who is not a relative, or a householder’s wife, offers robes out of their own free will in great quantity, that bhikṣu, if he wishes to accept them, may receive them up to the measure of the upper and lower robes.
If one accepts more than that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a monk, for a layman or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, has the price for a robe prepared with the thought:
'With such and such a price for a robe, I shall buy such and such a robe and give it to a certain monk. "

"Previously, this bhikṣu did not exercise his right of self-indulgence; yet, for the sake of a fine robe, he created a slight pretext and went to the place of a householder or a householder’s wife who was not a relative, saying to them:
'It is well of you!'"
‘Prepare such and such a price for a robe and buy such and such a robe for me, so that it may be of good quality.
If she obtains such a robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative has each prepared the price for a robe, thinking:
'With such and such a price for a robe, I shall buy such and such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu. "

"Suppose that monk, having not previously been invited to accept gifts at his own discretion, for the sake of fine robes, creates even a slight pretext and goes to the home of a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, and speaks to them thus:
'It is well of you!'"
"Prepare such and such a price for robes and buy one suitable robe for me, so that it may be fine.
If she obtains such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has a messenger sent by a king, a royal minister, a brahmin, or a householder to deliver the price for a robe;
and that messenger arrives at the bhikṣu's location and says to him:
'Venerable sir, do you know of this?'"
‘If this price for robes has been sent by a king, a royal minister, a brahmin, or a householder,
Venerable Sir, please accept this price for robes.
The bhikṣu should speak to the messenger as follows:

“Monks, it is not the rule that we should accept the price of robes; rather, when we require robes and obtain pure robes, we should take the goods with our own hands and quickly make and keep them as robes.”
The messenger said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
Is there an attendant who can constantly perform services for the bhikṣus?"
The bhikṣu in need of robes should point out an attendant, a guardian of the monastic quarters, or a lay follower (upāsaka), and say to them:
"These people are always able to serve as attendants for the bhikṣus."
The messenger goes to the person in charge and says to him:
"Excellent, steward!
With such and such a price for robes, purchase such and such a robe and give it to the bhikṣu so-and-so."
"When the time comes for that bhikṣu to need robes, he shall come, and I shall give him the robes.
Having either exhorted the person himself or sent someone else to exhort them, he returns to where the bhikṣu is and, having arrived, says:
"Venerable sir, I have finished exhorting the official whom you indicated."
"Venerable one!
When you require robes, go and take them; we shall give robes to the Venerable.
The monk who requires robes should go to the place of the attendant and request robes, saying these words:
"I need a robe! I need a robe!
He requested thus a second and a third time.
If one obtains the robe, it is well;
if not, one should stand silently before the distributor for a fourth, fifth, and at most a sixth time.
If one stands before the distributor for a fourth, fifth, and at most a sixth time, and obtains the robe, it is well.
If he does not obtain [the robe], yet seeks it further beyond this limit for the sake of obtaining a robe, and if he should obtain that robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go himself or send a messenger to the place from which the price of the robe came, and speak thus:

"You sent the price of a robe for a certain bhikṣu; that bhikṣu has not been able to use your robe-price at all. You yourself should take care of your property so that it is not lost; such is the rule."
“If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding from *kōśeya* silk, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding from pure black sheep’s wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.”
“If a bhikṣu wishes to make a new sitting mat, he should use two parts of pure black wool from a ram, a third part white, and a fourth part inferior wool.

If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat without using two parts of pure black wool, one-third part white, and one-fourth part inferior wool, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).

"If a bhikṣu wishes to make a new sitting mat, he must necessarily keep his old sitting mat for a full six years. If, within those six years, the bhikṣu—whether he has discarded the old sitting mat or not—makes another new sitting mat, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha."
"If a bhikṣu wishes to make a new *niṣīdana*, he must take from each of the four sides of the old *niṣīdana* a span of the Sugata’s measure, in order to destroy its fine color."
If a bhikṣu, for the sake of beauty, does not take an old *niṣīdana* and disfigure it by trimming each of its four edges by one *śugata-vidatthi*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a road, obtains wild sheep’s wool and wishes to accept it, that bhikṣu may take it with his own hands for up to three *yojanas*.

If there is no one to carry it for him beyond that distance, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wild sheep’s wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu takes gold or silver with his own hand, or causes another to take it, or instructs another to take it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu purchases various goods with gold or silver, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms-bowl, he may do so for up to ten days; if he keeps it longer than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, whose bowl has not yet reached five mends, seeks a new bowl for the sake of its excellence, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
That bhikṣu must relinquish that bowl before the community of bhikṣus; the lowest bowl among those in the community of bhikṣus should then be given to him."
One should instruct him thus:
"O Bhikṣu, that you have received this bowl until it is broken is the natural course of things.
"If a bhikṣu himself begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"If a monk, for whom a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative has had a weaver weave a robe, and that monk—without having been previously invited by them—approaches the weaver on account of a minor pretext for the sake of obtaining a fine robe and says to the weaver:
'Do you know? "
"This robe is being made for me; weave it well so that it is dense and wide, and I shall perhaps give you a small gift.

If that bhikṣu, having either exhorted the weaver himself or caused another to exhort him, subsequently gives a small gift—even a single meal, or an item for a meal, or the equivalent value of a meal—for the sake of obtaining the robe.
If he obtains this robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to another bhikṣu, and later, out of anger, resentment, and displeasure, either takes it back himself or causes another to take it back, saying:
'Bhikṣu, give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.'"
This is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This bhikṣu must relinquish this robe before the other bhikṣus.

"If a bhikṿu, when ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, receives an urgent gift of robes, and that bhikṣu needs a robe, he may take the goods with his own hand and keep them until the time for robes."
If one keeps them beyond this limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, during the three months of the summer retreat when an intercalary month occurs, has not yet completed eight months;

and if that bhikṣu dwelling in an *āraṇya* (forest) hermitage has doubts, fears, or apprehensions regarding safety, and if he wishes to place any one of his three robes inside a village dwelling, or if, for some reason, he must go outside the boundary and stay apart from his robe, he may do so for a maximum of six nights."
If it exceeds one night, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when one month of spring remains, should seek a rain-bath robe; he may keep it for half a month."
If a bhikṣu, within the final month of spring, seeks a rain-bath robe and keeps it for more than half a month, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a donor intends to give property to the Saṃgha, diverts it to himself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣu, for whom the Buddha has permitted the consumption of the four kinds of medicinal substances to be held and swallowed—
namely, ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar—
keeps these medicines overnight after they have been consumed by a sick bhikṣu, he may consume them for a maximum of seven days. If he exceeds seven days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.”
"Venerable sirs!
The thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas have been recited.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in regard to these?"
"A second and third time, he asks in the same manner:
'Venerable sirs!
Since you are pure in this matter, as indicated by your silence, let it be so held.'"
"Venerable sirs!
These ninety *pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*.
'If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*.'"
“If a bhikṣu speaks disparagingly, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu engages in double-tongued speech to incite strife among other bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that the Saṃgha has already settled a matter in accordance with the Dharma, should reopen it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, he commits a pāyattika offense;
except when a man of intelligence is present."
"If a bhikṣu teaches unordained persons using the verses and phrases of the *Chanda-gāthā*, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, before an unordained person, speaks of a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) for his own sake—whether he knows it or sees it—and claims, 'I know thus;
I see thus,' [it is a pāyattika]."
"...up to: if it is true, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika;
except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha."
"If a bhikṣu first listens with approval and later says:
'The bhikṣus have distributed the property of the Saṃgha according to their personal intimacy,' it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, should speak thus:
'What is the use of reciting these minor and trifling precepts?

Because these precepts are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa, the minds of the bhikṣus become remorseful, corrupted, distressed, and feverish; they become sorrowful and unhappy, giving rise to a mind that turns away from the precepts.'"
"To thus disparage and revile the precepts constitutes a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu kills various plants and grasses, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu scolds or abuses [another], it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu, being asked a question, does not answer and thereby annoys another, it is a pāyattika.

“If a bhikṣu, having spread out or caused another to spread out on an open space bedding belonging to the Saṃgha—whether a sitting bench, a sleeping bed, a hook-restraint, or a seat-cum-bedding—and sits or lies upon it, and when departing neither picks it up himself nor instructs another to pick it up, it is a pāyattika.”

"If a bhikṣu spreads bedding or mats within a bhikṣu’s dwelling—whether spreading them himself or having someone else spread them—and sits or lies upon them, yet when departing does not remove them himself nor instruct another to remove them, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, within a bhikṣu’s dwelling, being angry, resentful, and displeased, either drags himself out or causes another to drag him out, saying:
'Get out!'"
"Be extinguished!
You should not dwell herein.
Because of these causes and conditions, it is no different [from the previous offense], and constitutes a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, in a bhikṣu’s dwelling, knowing that other bhikṣus have already settled there and finished laying out their bedding and mats, later comes and forcibly lays out bedding himself or causes others to lay it out, thinking:
'If they do not like it, they shall leave of their own accord.'"
Because of these causes and conditions, it is no different [from the previous offense], and it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, on an upper story of a bhikṣu’s multi-storied building, sits or lies down with force upon a chair with pointed legs or a bed, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living organisms, pours it onto grass or soil himself, or causes another to pour it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu wishes to construct a large dwelling, he may build it up gradually from the ground level toward the door and windows, stacking two or three layers to ensure it is firm."
If one crosses over the ramparts, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, not appointed by the Saṃgha, instructs a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu, though appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct a bhikṣuṇī, continues until sunset, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu speaks thus:
'The bhikṣus instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of gain and offerings,' it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu travels along a road in company with a bhikṣuṇī, even as far as a single village, it is a pāyattika, except in cases of necessity.
'Cases of necessity' refers to when there are many companions, or when there is suspicion or fear along the route; these are called cases of necessity."
"If a bhikṣu, having made an agreement with a bhikṣuṇī, boards a boat together with her, whether going upstream or downstream, it is a pāyattika,
except for crossing directly across."
"If a bhikṣu gives clothing to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu makes clothing for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a bhikṣuṇī in a secluded, concealed place, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an open, unconcealed place, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu, knowing that food was obtained through the instigation of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise, eats it, he commits a pāyattika offense;
except in cases of prior wholesome causes and conditions from when he was a layman.
“If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, he commits a pāyattika offense.”
Except in cases of special circumstances.
Special circumstances refer to the time of illness and the time of receiving a gift of robes; these are called special circumstances.
"If there is a place where a meal is offered, a monk who is not ill should eat only one meal."
"If one exceeds one meal, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson and they offer him food at his pleasure, whether cakes or parched grain,
the bhikṣus may accept two or three bowls if they have need of them."
If one takes more than this, it is a pāyattika offense.
After receiving two or three bowls, one should go outside and give them to other virtuous bhikṣus; this is the natural rule of the Dharma.
"If a bhikṣu, having finished eating, eats again without having received the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the practice of receiving leftover food), it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has finished eating and has not received the *khalupaścādbhakti*, forcibly encourages him and offers him much food and drink, saying:
'Bhikṣu, eat!'"
If, out of malice, one forms this thought:
"May this bhikṣu suffer distress for even a short while," then by reason of that cause, it is no different [from the offense]; it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu eats apart from the community, it is a pāyattika, except in cases of special circumstances. Special circumstances are:

when one is ill, when making robes, when about to travel by road, when about to travel by boat, during a great assembly, or when food is offered by non-Buddhist śramaṇas; these are called special circumstances."
“If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu eats food that has been stored overnight, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu places food or drink that has not been formally offered into his mouth, it is a pāyattika.”
Except for water and tooth-sticks:
"If a bhikṣu, among various families, [receives] such fine foods as milk,
curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, fish, or dried meat, and if that bhikṣu is not ill, seeks such fine foods for his own body, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu knowingly takes and uses water containing living beings, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu sits on a bed or seat within a house where a meal is being served, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, while eating at a layperson's home, sits insistently alone with a woman in a place for reclining, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a naked ascetic, whether a male renunciant or a female renunciant, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu goes to view an army on its march, it is a pāyattika,
except for a specific cause.
If a bhikṣu has a specific cause to go into an army, he may stay there for up to two nights."
If one stays for more than one night, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu stays within an army for even two nights, and observes the army setting out, the banners and standards of the generals, or the arraying of the troops for battle, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu, strikes him with his hand in a fit of rage and displeasure, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu, punches him with his hand in a fit of rage and displeasure, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it for even a single night, he commits a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir, come to the various households; they will provide you with much delicious food and drink.'"
That bhikṣu does not give food to that other bhikṣu, but speaks thus: "Go away!
It is not pleasant for me to sit or speak with you; it is pleasant for me to sit alone and speak alone."
If, wishing to cause annoyance, one forms this thought:
"May this bhikṣu be annoyed, even if only for a short time," then by reason of this cause and condition, it is no different; it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, desires to warm himself in the open air by burning grass, wood, cow dung, or refuse—whether he burns them himself or causes another to burn them—it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having already granted his consent (*chanda*) for a formal monastic procedure (*saṃghakarma*) conducted according to the Dharma, subsequently revokes it, he commits a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu stays overnight in the same room as a person who has not received full ordination for more than two nights, he commits a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu should speak thus:

'I understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma in this way: practicing the dharmas that obstruct the path does not actually obstruct the path,' those bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu in this manner:"
"Venerable sir!
Do not speak these words:
'I understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma in such a way that practicing the dharmas which obstruct the path cannot actually obstruct the path.'"
"Do not slander the Buddha, do not misrepresent the Buddha; it is unwholesome to slander the Buddha.
The Buddha does not speak such words. Through various causes and conditions, the Buddha has taught that the practices which obstruct the path truly do obstruct the path."
"O Venerable One!
Abandon this evil and false view.
When the bhikṣus have thus admonished that bhikṣu, if he persists in this matter and does not abandon it, the bhikṣus should admonish him a second and a third time.
"It is well if he relinquishes this matter;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu knows that a person has spoken thus and has not repented according to the Dharma, and because he has not relinquished this evil false view, he expels him."
If one keeps [a novice] to work with, speak with, or sleep with him, it is a pāyattika.
"If a śrāmaṇera should say:
'I understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma in this way: practicing various sensual desires cannot obstruct the Path.'"
The bhikṣus should instruct that śrāmaṇera in this way:
"You, śrāmaṇera!
Do not speak such words."
"I understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma in this way: the practice of various sensual desires cannot obstruct the Path.
Do not slander the Buddha; do not misrepresent the Buddha, for to slander the Buddha is unwholesome.
"The Buddha does not speak such words; through various causes and conditions, the Buddha has taught that the pursuit of sensual desires can obstruct the Path.
You, śrāmaṇera, must abandon this evil and heterodox view.
When the bhikṣus instruct the śrāmaṇera in this manner, if he persists in holding to it and refuses to relinquish it, the bhikṣus should instruct him a second and a third time.
"It would be well if you relinquish this matter;
if you do not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should speak to you thus:
'You, śrāmaṇera!'"
From this day forward, you should not say,
"The Buddha is my teacher," nor should you follow behind the bhikṣus.
Other śrāmaṇeras may stay with bhikṣus for even one or two nights, but you have no such right.
You fool, get out! Begone!
"Do not dwell herein.
If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled, yet he keeps him and allows him to stay in a single room, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu takes a jewel or what is considered a jewel, whether he takes it himself or tells someone else to take it, it is a pāyattika."
Except within a monastic dwelling or a residential quarters.
Whether it be precious objects or what is considered precious, if such things are within a monastic dwelling or a residential quarters, one should form this thought:
"To whom does this belong?"
"The owner has taken it away.
Such is the nature of things.
"If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he should apply one of the three types of discoloration to it: [one of] these three discolorations."
Whether it be blue, mud-color, or madder-brown—
if a bhikṣu makes a new robe without applying one of these three types of discolored dyes—
whether blue, mud-color, or madder-brown— it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu bathes within the half-month, it is a pāyattika, except for special circumstances.
Special circumstances refer to the remaining one month and a half of spring and the first month of summer; these two months and a half are called the 'hot season.'"
Except in cases of illness, during wind or rain, while working, or while traveling on a journey—these are called the *pratyaya* (circumstances).
"If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu intentionally causes another bhikṣu to feel doubt, thinking:
'May this bhikṣu be troubled for even a short time,' and because of this cause and condition,
it is no different [from the offense], it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu tickles with his fingers, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu stays overnight in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu intentionally terrifies another bhikṣu, or causes another to be terrified, even in jest, it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣu hides from another bhikṣu any of these personal requisites—whether it be a bowl, a robe, a door-bolt, leather sandals, or a needle-case—even one such item at a time, whether he hides it himself or causes another to hide it, even in jest, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having given robes to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, should immediately take them back for his own use, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, with groundless charges of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, slanders another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu travels along a road together with a woman, even as far as a single village, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu conspires with a group of thieves to travel together on the road, even as far as a single village, it is a pāyattika.
Seventy: "If a bhikṣu confers full ordination upon a person who is less than twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika."
Such a person does not obtain the precepts, and the bhikṣus may also censure him; such is the nature of the Dharma.
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, or causes another to dig it, or points it out, saying: 'Dig here.'"
"Pāyattika. If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for the four-month *pravāraṇā*, and accepts it beyond that period, it is a pāyattika,
except for a regular *pravāraṇā* invitation, except for a repeated *pravāraṇā* invitation, and except for an individual *pravāraṇā* invitation."
"If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, speaks thus:
'I have not yet studied this precept; first I shall question those bhikṣus who recite the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.'"
This is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu desires to obtain the benefit of the Dharma, he should train in this *prātimokṣa* and should also question those bhikṣus who recite the *sūtra*, the *vinaya*, and the *abhidharma*, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"What is the meaning of these words?
This is the nature of things.
"If a bhikṣu, while various bhikṣus are quarreling, disputing, and contending, stands silently in a secluded place to listen, thinking thus:"
"I shall remember and uphold whatever the bhikṣus say"—
this is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, while the Saṃgha is settling a matter, rises and leaves in silence, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu treats another bhikṣu with contempt, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed a virtuous bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
Except in cases of necessity.
"If a bhikṣu, having been invited for a meal, goes to another house before or after the meal, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu passes by the gate or near the gate of a Kṣatriya king who has been consecrated with the water-sprinkling ceremony, while the night is not yet over and the treasures have not yet been put away, it is a pāyattika."
Except for a major cause.
"If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, speaks thus:
'I have only now learned that this rule is recited in the Sūtra of the Precepts every half-month.'"
If the other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has sat through two or three recitations of the precepts, let alone more, he cannot escape by claiming ignorance.
He shall be dealt with according to the Dharma for the offense he has committed and should be rebuked so as to bring him to remorse:
"Venerable sir!..."
You have suffered a loss and gained no benefit; you are unskilled. When the precepts were being recited, you did not listen with respect, nor did you think:
"This is indeed the case.
You did not hold it in high regard, you did not take it to heart, you did not attend to it with a single mind, and you did not listen to the Dharma with attentive ears regarding that matter.
“[If a monk does so, it is] a pāyattika. ‘If a monk makes a needle case out of bone, tooth, or horn, it is a pāyattika.
‘If a monk wishes to make a sitting bed or a sleeping bed, the legs should be eight finger-breadths high, excluding the space for the mortise.”
If one exceeds [the prescribed measure], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu himself stores tūla-cotton in a mattress, or causes another to store it, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu wishes to make a rain-bath robe, it should be measured according to these proportions:
its length shall be six spans of the Sugata’s hand, and its width shall be two and a half spans of the Sugata’s hand.”
If one exceeds these measurements, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu wishes to make a robe to cover the body, he should measure it; the measurement for this is:
four sugata-spans in length and two and a half sugata-spans in width."
If one exceeds these measurements, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu wishes to make a niṣīdana (sitting mat), he should measure it; the measurement for this is:
two spans of the Sugata in length and one and a half spans of the Sugata in width."
If one adds even a span’s width of thread or makes it exceed [the prescribed measure], it is a *pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in measure to the Buddha’s robe, or exceeds the measure of the Buddha’s robe, it is a *pāyattika*.”
Regarding the measurement of a Buddha’s robe within this context:
it is nine Sugata-spans in length and six Sugata-spans in width; this is called the measurement of a Buddha’s robe.
"Venerable sirs!..."
The ninety *pāyattika* rules have already been recited.
Now I ask the venerable ones: "Are you pure in this matter?
A second and a third time he asks in the same manner.
"Venerable sirs!
Since you are silent, you are pure in this matter; thus it shall be held.
"Venerable sirs!"
These four *pātideśanīya* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*:
"If a bhikṣu, being not ill, receives food with his own hand from a non-relative bhikṣuṇī inside a layperson’s house, that bhikṣu must confess his offense before the other bhikṣus, saying:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"I have fallen into a blameworthy state that should not have been done; this is a dharma from which one may emerge, and I now emerge from it.
This is the first *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.
"There are certain bhikṣus who have been invited to a meal at the home of a layperson; while there, one bhikṣuṇī stands by and points out:
'Give rice to this bhikṣu, give soup to that bhikṣu.'"
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Wait a moment, sister!
Wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating."
"If there is not even a single bhikṣu among the assembly of bhikṣus who can say to that bhikṣuṇī:
'Sister, wait a moment!
Wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating.'"
That bhikṣu should confess his offense before another bhikṣu, speaking thus:
"Venerable sirs!
I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma that ought not to be committed; this is a dharma that may be confessed, and I now confess it."
This is the second *pāṭidesanīya* rule.

“If there is a family under training (*śaikṣa-kula*) for which the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of designating it as a family under training (*śaikṣa-kula-karman*), and if a bhikṣu, knowing that this is a family under training for which the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of designation, goes there uninvited and personally receives food with his own hands, that bhikṣu must confess his offense before another bhikṣu, saying:
‘Venerable sir!...’”
"I have fallen into a blameworthy state that ought not to have been done; this is a state from which one may emerge, and I now emerge from it.
This is the third *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.
"There is a monk residing in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) who experiences doubt and fear.

If a bhikṣu already knows that such a forest hermitage is subject to doubt and fear, and the Saṃgha has neither performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) nor permitted him to receive food and drink outside the vihāra—yet he receives food and drink inside the vihāra—that bhikṣu must confess his offense before another bhikṣu, speaking thus:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"I have fallen into a blameworthy state that ought not to have been done; this is a state from which one may emerge, and I now emerge from it.
This is the fourth *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.
"Venerable sirs!
The four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas have been recited.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in regard to these?"
"A second and third time, he asks in the same manner:
'Venerable sirs!
Since you are pure in this matter, as indicated by your silence, let it be so held.'"

These are the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma), which are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa:
‘One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe too high.’”
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear my inner robe too low.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear my inner robe unevenly.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear my inner robe like the head of a wood-chopping axe.'"
"One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe like a palm leaf;
one should train oneself not to wear the inner robe like an elephant's trunk;
one should train oneself not to wear the inner robe like a ball of roasted flour."
"One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe with small pleats.
One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe like two ears.
One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe in a billowing manner."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear the inner robe loosely or with gaps.
One should train oneself: 'I shall wear the inner robe evenly all around.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not let the upper robe hang too high.'"
"One should train oneself not to wear the robe pulled down.
One should train oneself not to wear the robe unevenly.
One should train oneself to wear the robe properly adjusted."
"One should train oneself: 'I will enter the homes of laypeople with my body well-covered.
One should train oneself: 'I will sit in the homes of laypeople with my body well-covered.
One should train oneself: 'I will enter the homes of laypeople in a proper manner.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall sit properly in the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with a sidelong glance.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with a sidelong glance.'"
"One should train oneself not to sniff while entering the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself not to sit while sniffing in the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson with an air of self-importance."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with an arrogant air.
One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the house of a layperson with a low voice.
One should train oneself: 'I shall sit in the house of a layperson with a low voice.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson while squatting on the heels.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson while squatting on the heels.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my head covered.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my head covered.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my turban wrapped around my head.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my turban wrapped around my head.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with hands on my hips.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with hands on my hips.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson exposing my chest.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my chest exposed.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my side exposed.
(40) One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my side exposed.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my robe tucked up over one shoulder.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my robe tucked up over one shoulder.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my robe tucked up on both sides.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a white-robed layperson with my robes tucked up on either side.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a white-robed layperson with my robes trailing and flapping.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a white-robed layperson with my robes trailing and flapping.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not swing my arms when entering the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit with swinging arms in the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not shake my shoulders when entering the house of a layperson.'"
50. “One should train oneself: ‘I shall not sit in the house of a layperson while shaking my shoulders.
One should train oneself: ‘I shall not enter the house of a layperson while shaking my head.
One should train oneself: ‘I shall not sit in the house of a layperson while shaking my head.’”
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the dwelling of a layperson swaying the body.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the dwelling of a layperson swaying the body.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the dwelling of a layperson with hands clasped together.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with hands clasped.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson limping.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson limping.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my feet crossed.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my feet crossed.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson resting my cheek on my hand, lest it cause the layperson to laugh.'"
"One should train in receiving rice with a single-minded focus.
One should train in receiving soup with a single-minded focus.
One should train in receiving rice and food without overflowing the bowl."
"One should train in eating soup and rice together.
One should train in not scooping out food from one side of the bowl.
One should train in not picking out the best portions of rice and food from within the bowl."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not take large mouthfuls of food.
One should train oneself: 'I shall eat mouthfuls of food that are of proper size.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not open my mouth while waiting for food.'"
"One should train oneself not to speak while eating.
One should train oneself not to bite off half a morsel of food.
One should train oneself not to make a chewing sound while eating."
"One should train oneself not to eat food by stuffing the mouth completely.
One should train oneself not to eat food by licking the lips while swallowing.
One should train oneself not to eat food by sticking out the tongue."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat food while smelling it.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat food while licking my hands.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat food while wiping the bowl with my fingers.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not discard food.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not shake my hand while eating.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not receive a vessel for food with soiled hands.'"
"One shall train oneself: 'One must not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more.
One shall train oneself: 'When not ill, one must not seek out soup or rice for one's own sake.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not look into the bowl of my neighbor with a jealous mind.
One should train oneself: 'I shall eat while observing the bowl with single-minded attention.
One should train oneself: 'I shall eat in proper sequence.'"
"One should not discard bowl-washing water inside the residence of a layperson, except when informing the donor; this is how one should train.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person riding a horse, except when they are ill; this is how one should train."
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is in front and a bhikkhu is behind, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: 'If a person is on the path and a bhikkhu is off the path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except when they are ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is standing high and a bhikṣu is below, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except when ill.
One should train oneself: 'If a person is sitting and a bhikṣu is standing, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is lying down and a bhikṣu is sitting, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If a person has their head covered, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is wearing a *bōtō* (a cloth head-wrap), one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If a person has their hands on their hips, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'If a person reveals their chest, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If a person reveals their side, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
100. “One should train oneself: ‘When a person has their robe tucked up over one shoulder, I shall not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: ‘When a person has their robe tucked up over both shoulders, I shall not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.’”
"One should train oneself: 'If a person has their robes trailing on the ground, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If a person is wearing sandals, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person wearing leather sandals, except in the case of illness; this is a training to be observed.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a staff, except in the case of illness; this is a training to be observed."
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is holding a parasol, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If a person is holding a five-foot sword, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is holding a small knife, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If a person is holding a bow, arrows, or various other weapons, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should not discharge feces, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva upon living grass, except when ill; this is how one should train.
One should not discharge feces, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva into pure water, except when ill; this is how one should train."
"One should not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill; this is how one should train.
One should not climb a tree higher than a person's height, except for a weighty reason; this is how one should train."
"Venerable sirs! The rules of training for the multitude have been recited. Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard?

"Venerable sirs!
Since you are silent, you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held.

These seven methods for settling disputes are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa:
"To one who should be granted the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence), the *saṃmukhavinaya* should be granted."
"To one who should be granted the *smṛtivinaya*, the *smṛtivinaya* should be granted.
To one who should be granted the *amūḍhavinaya*, the *amūḍhavinaya* should be granted."
"To those for whom confession (*pātimokkha-thapana*) is appropriate, one should grant confession.
To those for whom the search for the characteristics of the offense (*tassapāpiyasika*) is appropriate, one should grant the search for the characteristics of the offense.

To those for whom the further search for the characteristics of the offense (*tassapāpiyasikā-tassapāpiyasika*) is appropriate, one should grant the further search for the characteristics of the offense."
"One should train oneself thus: 'When various disputes arise within the Saṃgha, they shall be settled by the method of "covering with grass," just as one covers grass upon the ground.
Venerable sirs, the seven principles for settling disputes have been recited; now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?"
"A second and third time, he asks in the same manner:
'Venerable sirs!
Since you are pure in this matter, as indicated by your silence, let it be so held.'"

“Venerable sirs, the introduction to the precepts has been recited; the four *pārājika* dharmas have been recited; the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas have been recited; the two *aniyata* dharmas have been recited; the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas have been recited; the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas have been recited; the four *prātideśanīya* dharmas have been recited; the *saikṣa* dharmas have been recited; and the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* dharmas have been recited. These matters are contained within the Buddha’s Sūtra on the Precepts, which is recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*, as well as within the other precepts that follow the Path.”
"In this matter, O Venerable Ones!
You should train yourselves with a single mind in joyful harmony, free from contention, living in peace and happiness like water and milk mingled together.
Thus did the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipassī, surrounded by six million two hundred thousand bhikṣus, proclaim this Discourse on the Precepts.
"Patience is the supreme path; Nirvana is what the Buddha calls the highest.
One who causes affliction to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa.
Thus did the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śikhin, surrounded before and behind by eight hundred thousand bhikṣus, proclaim this precept-sūtra:
"Just as one with clear vision Is able to avoid dangerous and evil paths;
So too, in this world, those who are wise Are able to distance themselves from all evils.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin, surrounded before and behind by one hundred thousand bhikṣus, spoke this Sūtra of Precepts:
"Do no harm, do not speak ill of others; act according to what is taught in the precepts;
know moderation in eating; always delight in staying in secluded places;
with a pure mind, delight in diligence—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda, surrounded by forty thousand bhikṣus, spoke this precept-sūtra:
"Just as a bee gathers from flowers, Without harming their color or fragrance, It takes only the nectar and departs;
Thus should the sage dwell among the people."
"Do not obstruct the affairs of others; do not observe what is done or left undone.
Rather, observe your own conduct yourself, and scrutinize carefully what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
Thus spoke the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Konāgamana, surrounded by thirty thousand bhikṣus, as he recited this precept-sūtra:
"If you wish to attain a virtuous mind, do not be negligent; One should diligently study the wholesome Dharma of the Sages.
If there is one who knows tranquility and possesses single-mindedness, Only such a person can be free from sorrow and affliction."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa Buddha, surrounded by twenty thousand bhikṣus, spoke this precept-sūtra:
"Commit no evil whatsoever; Fully cultivate all wholesome dharmas;
Thoroughly purify your own mind— This is the teaching of all Buddhas."
I, Śākyamuni Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded before and behind by a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty unprecedented monks, have spoken this precept-sūtra:
"It is good to guard the body; it is also good to guard the speech.
It is good to guard the mind; it is good to guard all [the faculties]."
The bhikṣu who guards all [senses] shall be free from all evils;
the bhikṣu who restrains speech and mind and does not commit physical evils—
with these three paths of action purified, he attains the path realized by the Noble Ones.
"If a person beats or reviles you, do not retaliate; toward those who harbor resentment, let your heart feel no hatred;
amidst those who are angry, let your mind always remain pure; seeing others commit evil, do not do it yourself."
“The Seven Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who are able to rescue and protect the world—
this Sūtra of Precepts they have spoken, I have now fully expounded.”
The Buddhas and their disciples revere this Sūtra of Precepts;
having revered the Sūtra of Precepts, they each revere one another.
Endowed with a sense of shame and remorse, they are able to attain the unconditioned path.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Bhikṣus according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concludes: "The recitation of the precepts being finished, the Saṃgha shall perform the Poṣadha with a single mind."
